title: Starting to drink after forming his own band
summary: Cootie began drinking some two years after forming his band, drinking and then laying off, and quit entirely in the late 1950s.

story.theme_name: Drink, drugs and the bandstand's casualties
story.community_name: Drugs and drink on the bandstand and the road

blocks.x: Cootie, something that I didn't talk to you about. We've talked about all that time you were with Duke, and you never drank anything on the job, and so on. Oh, you never drank anything. And even with Goodman, you never drank anything. Well then, so, you got your own band together. What happened to you? You not only developed a taste for scotch, but was it a difference in your outlook, or what was it as well?
I don't know. Maybe handling men and seeing their reaction and going out on parties, with people inviting you out, and the thing that I never did drink. So I started to drinking.
Well, you mean in a way you were being like feted and everything. You were the star, really.

Yeah. And being, you know, invited out to different places, and I started to drinking. I'd have a drink here, a drink there and a drink there. So I acquired a taste for scotch. And so I started to hitting it. But --
Well, did this develop over two or three years, or something, you know, when you first had the band? Or
Oh, about two years after I had the band, I imagine.
Yeah.
But I never did drink steady. If I would drink two or three months, I would lay off two or three months.
Really?
Yeah.
Well, what would bring you to lay off?
I don't know.
-- that you were doing the wrong thing for yourself?
Yeah. Uh-huh. And check myself out. If I would drink this year, the next year I wouldn't drink.
No kidding.
Yeah.

Well, I know one thing that you said to me before somewhere, that drinking or smoking pot and so on, that you could labor under the delusion that you're helping your -- what you're playing and everything. But that this is an illusion. That it's not true.
No.
You're probably hurting what you're doing.

Yeah. And I found out that it makes you nervous. It works on the nervous system. I don't think you have the horn, the instrument under control, when -- when you're not drinking, I used to always have my instrument under control. And I found out that wasn't no good.
Yeah.
You know?
Yeah.
And that's the reason why I used to check myself, drink two or three months and lay off.
No kidding.
Yeah.

Well, besides that, there's the fact that if you're drinking, and if you're being entertained, and you're the star or whatever, and you're drinking, even if you don't know it at the time, you know it the next day, that maybe everything wasn't just exactly the way you wanted it to be, because as you say, you're not really in control. If you're drinking, you don't know exactly just, you know, you're maybe not acting just the way you would be doing if you weren't drinking.
That's correct. I don't see where alcohol ever helped anyone, unless they were sick.
Yeah.
And I've been around many persons that drank and drank and drank, and it half killed a lot of good

musicians. Famous musicians, alcohol has. And I see this thing has happened to them. And maybe, yes, when I look at them, and I see them, that's the reason I don't drink today, again. It's been about 18 years since I had a drink of alcohol.
18 years?
Uh-huh.
Has it really? No kidding. So back, like in '58 or something.
Yeah.
About the time that you began to have the small band? Am I right?
Yeah.
Were you still drinking when you had the seven pieces?
I think that's when I stopped drinking, I think.
Is it?
Yeah.
